name: Mustang & Dolpo
tagline: Walled Lo, Thakali villages and remote Dolpo
meta_description: Mustang & Dolpo: Lo Manthang, Muktinath, Kagbeni, Thakali villages, Phoksundo Lake and Dho Tarap, with seasons, permits, flights and trekking advice.
summary: Mustang and Dolpo lie north of the main Himalaya, in the rain shadow of Dhaulagiri and Annapurna. Lower Mustang has Jomsom, Muktinath and the Thakali villages; Upper Mustang has the walled city of Lo Manthang; Dolpo has Phoksundo Lake and Bon valleys. Go April–June or September–October; restricted permits apply north of Kagbeni and in Dolpo.
intro: This is the dry side of Nepal. North of Dhaulagiri and the Annapurnas the monsoon clouds run out of rain, and the land turns to red cliffs, grey scree and wind-carved canyons, broken by green squares of barley and apple orchards wherever a stream can be led onto a field. Upper Mustang gets only about 250–400 mm of rain a year. The people here speak Tibetan dialects and Thakali, and their gompas, chortens and mani walls belong to the Tibetan world.

Mustang follows the Kali Gandaki, the river that cuts between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I. Lower Mustang, from Tukuche and Marpha up to Jomsom, Kagbeni and Muktinath, lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area and is open to anyone with the usual permit. It is reached by a 20-minute flight from Pokhara or a long day by jeep. North of Kagbeni begins Upper Mustang, the old kingdom of Lo, a restricted area with its own costly permit.

Upper Mustang's villages, Ghami, Tsarang, Chhoser and the walled capital of Lo Manthang at about 3,840 m, were closed to foreigners until 1992. A jeep road now reaches Lo Manthang, but the walk in, four to five days from Kagbeni, is still the best way to understand the place: one village, one gompa and one high pass at a time, with the wind rising every afternoon.

Dolpo, west across the Dhaulagiri and Kanjiroba ranges, is harder to reach and much less visited. Flights go from Nepalgunj to Juphal, and from there everything is on foot. Lower Dolpo holds Phoksundo Lake at about 3,612 m and the Tarap valley; Upper Dolpo, beyond the high passes, holds Shey Gompa and villages where Bon and Buddhism are both practised. We plan Dolpo as camping treks of two to four weeks with a full crew.

story.title: Salt, kings and the valleys beyond the Himalaya
paras: For centuries the Kali Gandaki was a trade road. Caravans of yaks, mules and sheep carried salt and wool south from Tibet and brought grain, rice and cloth north from the Nepal hills, and Mustang's villages lived by taxing, storing and moving those loads. Around 1380 a ruler named Ame Pal founded the kingdom of Lo and its walled capital, Lo Manthang. His successors built the great gompas of Thubchen and Jampa in the 15th century and held Lo as a Tibetan-speaking kingdom, later a vassal of the Gorkha state.

Further south, the Thakali of the Thak Khola made the salt trade their business. From the late 19th century until about the late 1920s Thakali merchant families held the government customs contract for the trade, and Tukuche grew into the chief trading post, with large courtyard houses that still stand. When the trade with Tibet faded after 1959, many Thakali families moved south and became hoteliers and traders across Nepal, which is why Thakali food is now served in every Nepali town.

The 20th century closed and then opened the north. After 1959 Tibetan resistance fighters based themselves in Upper Mustang until they were disarmed in 1974, and the area stayed off limits to foreigners until 1992. Lo's king kept a ceremonial role until Nepal became a republic in 2008. Dolpo stayed remote: in 1973 Peter Matthiessen and the biologist George Schaller walked to Shey Gompa to study blue sheep, a journey Matthiessen told in The Snow Leopard.

Today the road up the Kali Gandaki reaches Lo Manthang and the Tibetan border at Korala, jeeps carry pilgrims to Muktinath in an hour from Jomsom, and lodges in Upper Mustang have private bathrooms. Dolpo has changed far less; a road reaches Dunai, but Phoksundo and the Tarap valley are still days on foot. Both regions face the same questions: how to keep young people at home, how to farm with less snow and more floods, and how to welcome visitors without losing the old life.

legend: Local legend in Lo says that when Guru Rinpoche, the eighth-century teacher Padmasambhava, passed through on his way to found Samye in Tibet, a demoness kept undoing the work of the faithful. He killed her near Ghami. Her blood stained the cliffs of Dhakmar red, her intestines became the long mani wall below Ghami, and her heart was buried at the place where Ghar Gompa, also called Lo Gekar, now stands. Pilgrims still walk this route in that order.
people: Thakali families live in Tukuche, Marpha and the Thak Khola, speaking Thakali and Nepali and running lodges, orchards and shops. Upper Mustang is home to the Loba, who speak Loke, a Tibetan dialect, and follow mainly the Sakya school of Buddhism. Dolpo's people, often called Dolpo-pa, farm barley at around 4,000 m and herd yaks; many follow Bon, the old Tibetan religion, and others Buddhism. Gurung and Tibetan families also live along the Kali Gandaki.

untold.fact: Upper Mustang, the old kingdom of Lo north of Kagbeni, was closed to foreign visitors until 1992. It still has a restricted-area permit with a fee far higher than other trekking areas in Nepal.

Shey Phoksundo National Park, established in 1984 and covering about 3,555 square kilometres of Dolpa and Mugu, is the largest national park in Nepal. It protects Phoksundo Lake, Shey Gompa and snow leopard habitat.
Jigme Dorje Palbar Bista, the last king of Lo, was born in Lo Manthang's palace in 1930. His title ended in 2008 when Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a republic. He died in 2016.
Mustang's valley walls hold some 10,000 man-made caves. The oldest were used as burial chambers as early as about 1,000 BC; later ones became homes, granaries and meditation cells.
Eric Valli's 1999 film Himalaya, about a salt caravan in Dolpo and acted mainly by Dolpo villagers, was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, representing Nepal.

taste.name: Thakali khana
taste.text: The Thakali set meal: rice or buckwheat dhindo, black lentil dal cooked with jimbu herb and ghee, greens, potato achar and often dried mutton, refilled until you stop. Eat it in a family kitchen in Tukuche, Marpha or Jomsom, with Marpha apples or apple brandy after.

highlights.title: Lo Manthang, the walled city of Lo
highlights.text: The capital of the old kingdom at about 3,840 m, with mud-brick walls, one gate, a five-storey palace and the 15th-century gompas of Thubchen and Jampa, whose murals were restored over many years. Give it two full days, with a ride out to the caves.

highlights.title: Tiji festival in May
highlights.text: Three days of masked dances by the monks of Chhoede gompa in Lo Manthang's square, telling how the deity Dorje Jono defeated a demon who brought drought to Lo. It usually falls in May; dates follow the Tibetan calendar, so check them each year.

highlights.title: Muktinath and its 108 spouts
highlights.text: A shrine at about 3,710 m sacred to Hindus as a place of Vishnu and to Buddhists as Chumig Gyatsa. Pilgrims run under 108 spouts of icy water and visit the flame that burns over water. Jeeps reach it from Jomsom in about an hour.

highlights.title: Kagbeni and the Thakali villages
highlights.text: Kagbeni's mud lanes and Sakya gompa at the door of Upper Mustang, Marpha's whitewashed lane and apple orchards, and Tukuche's old salt-trade houses under Dhaulagiri. Each sits a short drive or an easy walk from Jomsom, and each has a family kitchen worth the stop.

highlights.title: Sky caves of Chhoser and Dhakmar
highlights.text: Thousands of caves cut into Mustang's cliffs, used as tombs, homes and meditation cells over almost 3,000 years. At Chhoser you can climb inside the Jhong cave complex; near Ghami the red cliffs of Dhakmar are honeycombed with them.

highlights.title: Phoksundo Lake and the Tarap valley
highlights.text: In Dolpo, the turquoise lake at about 3,612 m behind the Bon village of Ringmo, inside Shey Phoksundo National Park, and the high farming valley of Dho Tarap at about 4,040 m. Both are days from any road, reached on foot from Juphal.

getting_there: For Mustang, fly from Pokhara to Jomsom, whose airport sits at about 2,720 m, in about 20 minutes. Flights leave only in the early morning, before the Kali Gandaki wind rises, and are often delayed; keep a spare day. By road, Pokhara to Jomsom is about 160 km and 7–9 hours by jeep via Beni, Tatopani and Ghasa, and the Beni–Ghasa section is prone to landslides in July and August. From Jomsom, jeeps reach Muktinath in 1–1.5 hours and Lo Manthang in 6–7 hours. For Dolpo, fly Kathmandu to Nepalgunj in about an hour, spend a night, then take an early flight to Juphal. From Juphal, Phoksundo Lake is three days on foot and Dho Tarap five to six. Check current status before you travel, as roads and flight schedules change each season.
permits: Lower Mustang, up to Kagbeni and Muktinath, needs the Annapurna Conservation Area permit, as we understand it NPR 3,000 for most foreigners, plus a TIMS card. Upper Mustang, north of Kagbeni, needs a restricted-area permit, USD 500 for the first 10 days and USD 50 for each extra day, issued only through a registered agency for at least two trekkers with a licensed guide. Upper Dolpo has the same fee; Lower Dolpo costs about USD 20 a week, plus the Shey Phoksundo National Park fee. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas must walk with a licensed guide. Fees are under review from time to time; check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Jomsom about −4 to 9 °C; dry, clear, strong afternoon wind
months.summary: January is the coldest month and the quietest. Lower Mustang stays open: Jomsom, Marpha and Kagbeni are dry and sunny by day, and Muktinath works for pilgrims who can take freezing nights and possible snow. Upper Mustang is bitter, and many families from Lo Manthang spend the winter further south, so lodges and gompas there may be closed. Dolpo's high passes are snowbound. Pokhara–Jomsom flights run on clear mornings.
months.tip: Stay in Lower Mustang and carry a down jacket for the evenings and the wind.

months.weather: Jomsom about −2 to 11 °C; mostly dry, some snow higher up
months.summary: February is still cold, with clear days and occasional snow at Muktinath and above. Thakali villages along the Kali Gandaki are quiet and welcoming, and Tukuche and Marpha make a good slow week with short walks and long kitchen meals. Losar, the Tibetan new year, falls in February or early March and is marked in Buddhist homes and gompas. Upper Mustang and Dolpo are not yet in season.
months.tip: Check road conditions to Muktinath after any fresh snowfall.

months.weather: Jomsom about 2 to 15 °C; warming, windy afternoons
months.summary: March opens the season in Lower Mustang. Days warm, apricot and apple blossom appears around Marpha and Kagbeni late in the month, and Muktinath pilgrim traffic grows. Upper Mustang lodges begin to reopen and Lo Manthang's families return, though nights there are still well below freezing. It is too early for Dolpo's passes. The afternoon wind in the Kali Gandaki is strong; plan walks for the morning.
months.tip: Walk the Kali Gandaki before about 11 am, when the wind begins.

months.weather: Jomsom about 5 to 18 °C; dry, clear mornings
months.summary: April is one of the best months for Mustang. Upper Mustang treks and jeep trips run in full, with clear mornings, mild days and very cold nights in Lo Manthang. Fields around Ghami and Tsarang are being ploughed and irrigated, and Muktinath is busy with Indian and Nepali pilgrims. Dolpo's lower trails open late in the month, but high passes still carry snow. Book Upper Mustang permits and good lodges early.
months.tip: Apply for the Upper Mustang permit through your agency weeks ahead in spring.

months.weather: Jomsom about 9 to 21 °C; dry, warmer, wind and dust
months.summary: May is Tiji month in Lo Manthang, three days of masked dances in the square, usually in May by the Tibetan calendar. The whole of Upper Mustang is in season, the barley is green, and the caves at Chhoser are easy to visit. Dolpo opens properly: Phoksundo Lake and the Tarap valley are in good condition by mid to late May. Pre-monsoon haze can soften mountain views.
months.tip: If you want Tiji, book about six months ahead; Lo Manthang's lodges fill quickly.

months.weather: Jomsom about 12 to 23 °C; mostly dry north of the Himalaya
months.summary: The monsoon arrives in Pokhara in June, but Upper Mustang and Dolpo lie in the rain shadow and stay largely dry. Treks to Lo Manthang and Phoksundo continue, and Dolpo's high pastures fill with herders and yaks. The trouble is getting there: Pokhara–Jomsom and Nepalgunj–Juphal flights are cancelled more often, and the Beni road starts to suffer landslides. Build in spare days at both ends.
months.tip: Allow two spare days for flights in and out during the monsoon months.

months.weather: Jomsom about 14 to 23 °C; light rain, cloud in the south
months.summary: July is the heart of the monsoon in the rest of Nepal, but beyond Kagbeni the sky is often clear and the fields green. Upper Mustang treks run with few other trekkers, and summer is a common season for the long Upper Dolpo traverse. Flights are the weak point, and the road below Ghasa is often blocked by landslides. Trails and lodges inside Upper Mustang are quiet and pleasant.
months.tip: Ask about the road below Ghasa before choosing to drive rather than fly.

months.weather: Jomsom about 13 to 22 °C; mostly dry, cloud and showers in the south
months.summary: August is still monsoon in the south but a fine month north of the Himalaya. Yartung, the horse festival at Muktinath, usually falls around the Janai Purnima full moon in August or early September, with races, dancing and pilgrims. In Dolpo, Shey's 12-yearly festival is next expected in 2036. Phoksundo and the Tarap valley are green and busy with herders. Flights and the Beni road remain unreliable.
months.tip: Check Yartung dates against the lunar calendar before you book.

months.summary: September starts the autumn season. Rain fades in the south, flights become more reliable as the month goes on, and Upper Mustang's barley turns gold before harvest. Marpha's apples ripen from late August into September. Dolpo is in excellent condition, with the passes between Phoksundo and Dho Tarap usually open. Yartung may fall in early September. A good month for quiet trails before the October rush.
months.tip: Plan late-September flights to avoid the last monsoon cloud over Pokhara.

months.weather: Jomsom about 5 to 18 °C; dry, clear, stable
months.summary: October is the classic month across the region: clear skies, settled weather and harvest in the fields. Upper Mustang and Lower Mustang are busy, Muktinath is busy with pilgrims, and Marpha's apple season continues. Dolpo treks finish before the passes turn cold. Nights in Lo Manthang drop below freezing by the end of the month. Book flights, permits and lodges early.
months.tip: Book Jomsom flights early; the Dashain holidays fill planes and jeeps.

months.weather: Jomsom about 0 to 14 °C; very clear, cold nights
months.summary: November brings the clearest air of the year and fewer visitors. Lower Mustang is excellent for walking between Jomsom, Kagbeni, Lubra and Muktinath, with sharp views of Dhaulagiri and Nilgiri. Upper Mustang is cold, and some Lo Manthang lodges close towards the end of the month. Dolpo's passes can get snow and most treks there end by early November. Pack for freezing nights.
months.tip: Check which Upper Mustang lodges are still open before a late-November trip.

months.weather: Jomsom about −3 to 11 °C; dry, clear, windy
months.summary: December is cold, dry and quiet. Lower Mustang works well for a short trip: fly to Jomsom, stay in Marpha or Tukuche, and drive up to Muktinath on a clear day. Upper Mustang is very cold and many residents leave for the winter; Dolpo is closed to most trekking. Flights are usually reliable in the clear weather, and the Thakali kitchens are warm.
months.tip: Pack warm layers for Muktinath, where the wind makes it feel far colder.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Mustang?
faqs.a: April to June and September to October are the best months for Upper Mustang, with clear mornings and open lodges; May adds the Tiji festival in Lo Manthang. Because Mustang lies in the rain shadow, June to August is also possible, though flights and the Beni road are less reliable. Lower Mustang, around Jomsom and Muktinath, works most of the year.

faqs.q: How do I get to Mustang from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly or drive to Pokhara, then fly about 20 minutes to Jomsom on an early-morning flight, or drive about 160 km and 7–9 hours via Beni. From Jomsom, jeeps reach Kagbeni in 30 minutes, Muktinath in about an hour and Lo Manthang in 6–7 hours. Flights are often delayed by wind or cloud; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the Upper Mustang permit?
faqs.a: As we understand it, the Upper Mustang restricted-area permit costs USD 500 per person for the first 10 days and USD 50 for each extra day, plus the Annapurna Conservation Area permit. It is issued only through a registered agency, for at least two foreigners travelling with a licensed guide. The fee has been reviewed more than once; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Mustang and Dolpo?
faqs.a: Yes. Upper Mustang, Lower Dolpo and Upper Dolpo are restricted areas where a licensed guide and a registered agency have long been required. Since April 2023 Nepal also requires foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas, including Lower Mustang and Shey Phoksundo, to walk with a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Lower and Upper Mustang?
faqs.a: Lower Mustang runs from the Thak Khola villages of Tukuche and Marpha to Jomsom, Kagbeni and Muktinath, and needs only the Annapurna Conservation Area permit. Upper Mustang, north of Kagbeni, is the old kingdom of Lo, with Ghami, Tsarang and Lo Manthang, and needs the costly restricted-area permit. Upper Mustang is higher, drier and more Tibetan in language and religion.

faqs.q: Can I drive to Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: Yes. A jeep road runs from Jomsom to Lo Manthang in about 6–7 hours via Kagbeni, Chele, Ghami and Tsarang, and Pokhara to Lo Manthang is possible in one very long day. The road is rough, dusty and can be cut by landslides or river crossings. You still need the restricted-area permit and a guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get to Phoksundo Lake in Dolpo?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Nepalgunj, about an hour, stay a night, then take an early flight of about 45 minutes to Juphal. From Juphal, walk three days via Dunai and Chhepka to Ringmo village and the lake at about 3,612 m. You need the Lower Dolpo permit, the Shey Phoksundo National Park permit and a licensed guide; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Tiji festival in Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: Tiji lasts three days in the third month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in May; in 2026 it is expected on 14–16 May. Monks of Chhoede gompa perform masked dances in the square in front of the palace. Dates move each year with the lunar calendar, so confirm them before booking flights and lodges.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness at Muktinath or Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: It is possible. Muktinath is at about 3,710 m and Lo Manthang at about 3,840 m, and flying to Jomsom then driving straight up gains height fast. Spend a night in Jomsom or Kagbeni first, drink plenty of water and avoid alcohol on the first nights. Headache that worsens, vomiting or breathlessness at rest mean you should descend.
